Field (Physics)

A field assigns a value (scalar, vector, tensor, or spinor) to every point in space–time.

  • “Field” here means a quantity defined at every point of space‑time (scalar, vector, tensor, spinor).
  • In quantum field theory, particles are excitations (quanta) of underlying fields (e.g., photons of the EM field, electrons of the Dirac field).
Field type Symbol / object Representative governing equation Canonical example
Scalar Φ(x)
(gravitational potential)		 ∇²Φ = 4πG ρ
(Poisson’s equation)		 Newtonian gravity in the weak‑field limit
Scalar T(x,t)
(temperature)		 ∂T/∂t = α ∇²T
(heat/diffusion equation)		 Heat conduction / diffusion
Vector E(x,t), B(x,t) Maxwell’s equations (SI):
∇·E= ho/ε0, ∇×E=-∂B/∂t,
∇·B=0, ∇×B=μ0J+μ0ε0∂E/∂t.		 Electromagnetic field
Tensor gμν(x) (metric) Einstein field eqs.:
Gμν + Λgμν = (8πG/c4) Tμν		 General relativity (gravity as spacetime geometry)
Spinor ψ(x)
(Dirac spinor)		 (iℏγμ∂μ - mc)ψ = 0
(Dirac equation)		 Electron field in quantum electrodynamics

Energy & momentum carried by fields (EM example)

  • Energy density: u = ( ε0 E^2 + B^2/μ0 )/2
  • Energy‑flux / momentum density (Poynting vector): S = (1/μ0) E × B (W·m−2)
